# Judging the team's work against my Phase 1 answer

## 1. Where I was wrong

I was wrong in one place, and it matters.

**The buyer.** In Phase 1 I said: VP or SVP Contact Center Operations signs. The CCO co-signs the suppression flag. The Retention Analytics person comes in year two for the feature export. The team's documents flag this exact question — "Decision 2 — it's yours: who is the buyer?" — and they leave the answer as Head of Retention Analytics, with the note that "consumed by existing retention modelling" points that way. They recognise the tension. They do not resolve it. They say: "This one is worth saying out loud on stage rather than swapping quietly — it changes who signs."

They are right that it changes who signs. They are wrong that it should stay with Retention Analytics. Here is the specific problem: the first deployment is a ranked queue on one desk (path 2) and, in my framing, an agent-brief screen. Both are operational. The person who manages the queue and the agents is the Contact Center Operations person. The Retention Analytics person's job is the propensity model, which is path 1, which is the destination, not the pilot. If the Retention Analytics person signs the contract, the first three months of the product are used by a team that didn't sign. The signatory's KPI (model performance, AUC, top-decile lift) is not the KPI that the first deployment affects (handle time, FCR, disposition code). The sales motion is: you sign, someone else uses it, and the value you are measured on doesn't move for two quarters. That is a motion that dies in procurement.

I was wrong to be so clean about "Operations signs, CCO co-signs, Analytics comes in year two." The real answer is: **Operations signs the first deployment. The CCO signs the suppression flag, which is in the first deployment. Analytics signs the feature export, which is the second deployment.** Three buyers, three budget lines, two deployments. The team's "one buyer, one product" framing is too narrow for what the product actually is.

Where their reasoning did *not* move me: the latency headline. They say "your propensity model refreshes monthly and never sees what the customer said. Ours moves the moment the transcript lands." I said the headline should be memory, not latency. They are right that the latency claim is structurally true and unattackable in the 18-minute format. I was right that it is only true for path 2 and contradicted by path 1. Both things are true. For the room, their headline is the better *sentence*. For the product, my framing is the better *architecture*. I would use their sentence in minute one and my framing everywhere else.

---

## 2. Where they are wrong

**The product is the score. It should be the brief.**

This is the central error, and it runs through every document. The score — the "conversation attrition score," ordinal, event-driven, bounded, decaying — is the product in their framing. The brief (the four items, the flag, the trajectory note on the agent's screen) is a *consumption path*. The flag (the suppression-list boolean) is a *sentence in Beat 4*. The score is what gets demoed, what gets measured, what goes into the model, what the back-test evaluates.

The evidence does not support the score as the product. The evidence supports the extraction and the accumulation. The ranking does not work: 8th of 9 on the whole portfolio, 0.115 vs 0.113 recall, indistinguishable from random. The dumb ledger — every scoring mechanism off — beats the full ledger on diffuse arcs. The confidence float, under the production model reader, is the *least* load-bearing mechanism; removing it changes 10.5% of the queue, less than the corroboration term. The scoring is not doing anything a simple count does not do, on the one stratum where accumulation works.

The extraction *does* work: 0.6549 recall, 5,723 of 5,736 quotes verbatim, 60 of 65 complaint escalation on the generic corpus, 29 of 29 "fired something" on card narratives. The accumulation *does* work: 30-0-0 on diffuse arcs, 239 of 485 entries worth more now than at write, 0 of 485 under unweighted count. The display *does* work: the agent reads four items in ten seconds, the case file is assembled, the quotes are verbatim.

The product should be: **extract, accumulate, display, flag.** The score is an intermediate representation. The brief is the output. The flag is the output. The score feeds the queue, but the queue is not the product. The brief is. The agent who reads the brief does not care what the score is. She cares what the customer said last time, in the customer's own words, with the date and the channel. The score is what the data scientist cares about, in year two, when the feature goes into the model.

They built the score as the product because the score is measurable. You can run a sign test on the score. You can compute top-decile uplift. You can report a p-value. You cannot run a sign test on "the agent handled the call in seven minutes instead of fourteen" without a before/after operational study that takes three months. So the score became the product because the score is the thing you can put in a slide. The brief became a consumption path because the brief is the thing you cannot measure in a back-test. This is the wrong reason, and it has distorted the product.

**The "day 74 and the customer isn't calling" answer is insufficient.**

Their answer: "We never contact them. We change what your agent knows the next time they do — and in cards, they do." The "and in cards, they do" is an assumption doing the work of a product feature. For a customer considering leaving, the next call may be the cancellation call. The brief helps on the cancellation call: the agent knows the history, offers the retention solution, the disposition code is "retention offer accepted" instead of "cancellation processed." But the 58 days in between are lost. The marketing email goes out. The cross-sell fires. The credit-line increase offer arrives. The customer who said "I'm not sure this card is worth it" in April gets an email in June saying "Congratulations! You qualify for a premium upgrade!"

The suppression flag saves those 58 days. It is a boolean in the CRM's suppression-list object. The marketing system checks it before sending. The customer does not get the email. The flag is not a sentence in Beat 4. It is a row in a table that the marketing platform queries. It is the thing that makes the "no outbound surface" claim *operational* rather than *rhetorical*. Without the flag, the "no outbound surface" claim means "Afterword cannot call the customer." With the flag, it means "the bank's marketing system will not call the customer, and here is the flag that makes that true." The first is a design choice. The second is a control. The CCO cares about the second.

They have the routing (`TRAJECTORY_TEAM`: distress → collections, life event → vulnerability, churn intent → retention) and the absence (no offer mechanism, no contact surface). They do not have the flag in the suppression list. The routing tells the *agent* where to send the case. The flag tells the *marketing system* not to send the email. These are different consumers, in different systems, with different triggers. The routing is in the code. The flag is not.

**The value chain is a ceiling, not a chain.**

They say $1.65M/year, multiply four haircuts through out loud, then say the chain has no false-positive leg, then say "say it as the gross ceiling before a precision haircut nobody has measured — or don't say a total at all." At that point, the $1.65M is a number you say out loud so they don't build a worse one in their head. That is a fair tactical reason. But the structure of Beat 5 still presents it as a chain you multiply through: five million accounts → 5% → 40% → 30% → 30,000 names → 10% save → $1.65M. The word "chain" implies a causal sequence. It is not causal. It is a ceiling with four unmeasured haircuts and no precision leg. The honest version is one sentence: "The maximum value is $1.65M/year if every one of the 30,000 names is a real leaver. We don't know what fraction is real. The back-test measures it." They get close. They do not say it as one sentence. They say it as a chain with a caveat, which is worse because the chain invites the question "but what's the save rate?" and the caveat says "we don't know," and the chain has already implied you do.

**The "58 days earlier" is a prediction claim wearing a structural costume.**

"Every tool on the market catches this call. On this arc we opened the case 58 days earlier." The "earlier" implies the event was going to happen. The event was authored to happen. The structural claim is: "the evidence for this customer's trajectory was complete on day 74. A per-call system would first flag it on day 132." That is true regardless of whether the customer actually leaves. The "58 days earlier" claim is true on this arc and false on any arc where the customer does not leave. They qualify it: "Say 'on this arc' every time." The qualification is necessary. It is not sufficient, because the CEO hears "58 days earlier" and thinks "you save me 58 days of lost margin per customer." The structural claim does not support that inference. The prediction claim does. And the prediction claim is not measured.

**The reader beat is the wrong evidence for the wrong audience.**

The model-vs-lexicon table (60/65 complaint escalation, 1/65 lexicon; 27/72 financial distress, 33/72 lexicon) is the answer to "what does the AI actually do?" It is not the headline. The headline is the product. The CEO does not care whether the reader is a model or a regex. The CEO cares whether the agent sees the right thing on screen. The reader beat is Q&A material. They know this: "Do not let the README's framing walk onto the stage." But the reader beat is in `01-THE-STORY.md`, which is the rehearsal document. The risk is that the rehearsed version of Beat 4 leads with the reader comparison, which is the right answer to "how does the reading work?" and the wrong answer to "why should I buy this?" The AI judge scores engineering quality separately. The CEO scores the product. These are different rooms, and the story document should be for the CEO.

**The deployment is not designed.**

The documents describe "the case briefs the next agent who speaks to them" and "a ranked queue on one desk." They do not describe the screen. What does the agent see? In Genesys, it is a custom desktop widget. In NICE, it is a panel in the Enlighten screen. In Salesforce CTI, it is a related list. In a bespoke desktop, it is an HTML iframe. The number of items, the layout, the refresh cadence, the integration with the existing screen-pop data: none of it is specified. The demo shows "the retro column" and "the day-0 remark" on a screen that is designed for the demo, not for the agent's desktop. For a CEO, the screen is the product. If the screen is not designed, the product is not designed. The 8-week deployment timeline they imply (fixed-fee back-test, then pilot) does not include the screen design, the CRM integration, the suppression-list wiring, or the desktop integration. Those are 3-4 of the 8 weeks, and they are the hard part.

---

## 3. What they missed entirely

**The suppression flag as a product feature.** Covered above. It is the single biggest omission. The flag is not in the product. It is a sentence in Beat 4 and a mapping in `TRAJECTORY_TEAM`. The product needs a flag that the marketing system checks. Without it, the UDAAP argument is rhetorical. With it, the UDAAP argument is operational. The CCO is not a co-signer. The CCO is a buyer with a different budget line and a different KPI (reduction in regulator-facing complaints, reduction in UDAAP findings, documented controls in the model risk file). The flag is the CCO's product. The brief is the Operations person's product. Two products, one engine, two buyers, two budget lines. They have one product, one buyer, one budget line.

**The data governance problem is a legal project, not a technical seam.**

They put the append-only ledger / no-delete problem in the objection playbook: "No good answer exists yet and do not invent one... Say: 'the prototype ledger is append-only; deletion is one of the seams that has to be built before any production integration, and it's on the list.'" This is the right thing to say in the room. But "a seam on the list" undersells it. The question is not "can we delete a row from the ledger?" The question is: "What is the legal retention obligation for the *derived* signals (the brief, the flag, the score) versus the *raw* transcript, and do they differ?" The bank's records-retention schedule (typically 5-7 years for call recordings under the risk-management framework) may require the transcript to be kept. The CCPA/CPRA right to deletion applies to personal information, which includes the transcript and the derived signals. GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure) applies if the bank has EU exposure. The question of whether a *derived* signal (a flag that says "financial distress, set 8/14, quote on file") can be deleted while the *source* transcript is retained is a legal question, not an engineering one. It requires a legal opinion from the bank's privacy counsel before the first sale. Budget: 2 weeks of legal time, 1 week of engineering (the voiding mechanism that marks entries as deleted but preserves the audit trail). They treat this as a technical gap. It is a legal gap, and it is the most likely reason the product does not go to production in the first 12 months.

**The "we can build this ourselves" objection.**

The objection playbook handles "isn't this in our structured data?" (good answer: competitor mention, payoff enquiry, life event have no structural proxy). It does not handle the more likely question from a CEO: "We have a data lake with 47 years of call recordings. We have a platform team of 40 engineers. Why can't we build this ourselves?" The answer is: you can. It is 6 months of platform-team time. The first deployment with us is 8 weeks. The extraction is the hard part, and it is a model call, not a data pipeline. The ledger is deterministic code, not a platform project. The screen is a CRM widget, not an architecture decision. The total build is 2 weeks of engineering for us (per Phase 1) plus 4-6 weeks of integration (CRM, suppression list, desktop). They do not say this because it is a sales objection, not a technical one, and the documents are technical documents. But the CEO will ask it. The answer should be: "Yes, you can build it. It is 6 months of your platform team. We do it in 8 weeks. The question is whether 6 months of your platform team is the best use of their time, or whether 8 weeks with us and a fixed fee is."

**The multi-bank / multi-product question.**

The documents are about one bank, one product line, one demo. The CEO will ask: "Can you do this for our mortgage book? Our auto loan book? Our small-business relationships?" The answer is: the engine is domain-independent. The content (signal families, phrase pools, thresholds) is re-authored per product line. The cost is a day of content authoring and under a dollar of model spend. The screen, the flag, the suppression-list wiring: all the same. The signal families change. The routing changes. The consuming desks change. They have this information in `04-ALTERNATE-STORIES.md` (thirteen directions, the cost to re-point). But it is framed as "alternate stories for the pitch," not as "the product works across product lines." The expansion path should say: "Phase 1: cards, one desk. Phase 2: cards, all desks (complaints, collections, retention). Phase 3: deposits, mortgages, auto, SMB. Same engine, different content, same screens." They have Phase 1 and "Phase 2: feature-store integration." The product-line expansion is missing from the deployment path.

**The operational measurement of the brief.**

The back-test measures the score: top-decile uplift, rank correlation, AUC. It does not measure the brief: handle time, first-call resolution, disposition code change, customer effort score. These are the metrics that the Operations person cares about and the Retention Analytics person does not. The back-test should have two success criteria: (1) the score's top-decile uplift in the propensity model (the Analytics person's metric), and (2) the disposition code change rate in the top-N flagged customers on the pilot desk (the Operations person's metric). They have (1). They do not have (2). The second is the metric that justifies the first deployment. The first is the metric that justifies the second deployment.

**What the demo must not do: they get this mostly right, but miss one thing.**

Their "never cut" list is good. Their "cut" list is good. The "what the demo must not do" is implicit in the tactical advice. What they miss: the demo must not show the *score* as the output. The demo should show the *brief* as the output. The score is what the system computes. The brief is what the agent reads. The retro column is what the system does to the old evidence. The score is a number. The brief is a document. The demo should end on the document, not the number. Their demo ends on "every tool on the market catches this call. On this arc we opened the case 58 days earlier." That is a number. It should end on the agent's screen: four items, one flag, one trajectory, the quote, the date. "This is what your agent sees before she picks up the phone." The number is the mechanism. The screen is the product.

---

## 4. The evidence, read hostilely

**What supports the central claim (the system reads, remembers, re-values, and displays):**

- **Extraction accuracy:** 0.6549 recall for the model reader across 10 datasets, 6,990 conversations. Quote fidelity: 5,723 of 5,736 verbatim. 11 non-verbatim, 2 relocated. This is strong. The model reads the transcript accurately and attaches the quote.
- **Complaint escalation detection:** 60/65 on the generic corpus. 23/24 on CFPB card narratives. This is the strongest signal family, and it is not the family the pitch is built on.
- **Retro re-scoring:** 239 of 485 entries are worth more now than at write. 0 of 485 under unweighted count. The mechanism does something a simple count does not. This is the core capability, and it is measured.
- **Reproducibility:** 908 tests, 903 pass. Byte-identical re-run from a different commit. Deployed pipeline agrees with local (eyeball, not test, but true as far as it goes). The model-swap (Nova vs Haiku) was done and measured for $0.027705.

**What is neutral:**

- **The 5-4-1, p=1.00 on the model reader at 200 customers.** Power failure, correctly labelled. Neither supports nor refutes.
- **The CFPB 29/29 "fired something on a marked document."** Strong sensitivity, but it is on complaint narratives, which over-represent complaint language. The specificity (26/35 exact type) is weaker. The n=8 for churn intent is too small to conclude anything.
- **The model-swap delta (4/282 coverage, 5/80 crossings).** 6.25% of crossings change. Not nothing. Not fatal. The protocol for handling it is written.

**What argues against the central claim as currently framed:**

- **The ranking does not work.** 8th of 9 on the whole portfolio. 0.115 vs 0.113 recall (random). On diffuse arcs: 30-0-0 vs the capped-memory arms, but 18-8-4 vs chance (p=0.076), and the dumb ledger beats the full ledger 18-7-5 (p=0.043), which becomes 13-11-6 (p=0.839) with randomised ties. The scoring mechanisms (decay, corroboration, cross-channel, escalation) are not adding signal beyond a simple count on the one stratum where accumulation works. The escalation bonus changes nothing at all (100% overlap on all 30 datasets).
- **The CFPB churn intent: 1/8.** The signal family the pitch rests on is the worst-performing family on the only real card data. n=8, post-hoc, complaint narratives. But the direction is bad, and the strong family (complaint escalation, 23/24) is the desk they are not selling to.
- **The 7x false-positive rate.** The model fires roughly 7x more unplanted extractions than the lexicon. Precision is unmeasured. On a 5-million-account book, 7x false positives on 30,000 true positives is 210,000 false positives. The chain does not price this.
- **The records reversed across two corpus rebuilds.** The results describe the corpus at least as much as the mechanism. This is the team's own language. It is the most honest sentence in the repo and the most damaging to the ranking claim.

**The critical distinction the evidence forces:**

The evidence supports **extraction + accumulation + display** (the brief). It does not support **extraction + accumulation + scoring + ranking** (the queue). The product should be the brief. The queue is a secondary feature whose ranking quality is not yet established. The back-test should measure the brief's operational impact (disposition code change, handle time) in addition to the score's model impact (top-decile uplift). If the ranking does not beat random, the queue is not the product. The brief is. The agent reads the brief regardless of the ranking. The ranking determines the order of the queue. The brief is useful whether it is first in the queue or fourteenth.

**Does the evidence base support my product, their product, both, or neither?**

It supports my product (the brief and the flag) more than it supports their product (the score and the queue). The extraction and accumulation work. The display works. The flag is not built but is trivially buildable from the existing routing. The ranking does not work. The score is an intermediate representation that the ranking depends on and the brief does not. The evidence says: build the brief, build the flag, and measure the operational impact. Do not build the queue as the product. Build the queue as a feature of the brief, for the desk that needs ordering.

---

## 5. Grading the self-criticism

This is rigour, not a substitute for rigour. The specific corrections — the $6,610 per-borrower error, the G.19 vs CORCCACBS correction, the SR 11-7 → SR 26-2 update, the "branch in code" → "routing plus absence" correction, the 7-10x → 3-9x multiple correction, the effective-yield 13.3% vs 22.15% correction — are the kind of corrections that change the numbers and change what gets said in the room. They are not performative. They are the work of a team that checked its own arithmetic and found errors. The fact that the $6,610 error was in the *original* pitch (quoting $1,464 gross interest on $6,610 per account alongside 608 million accounts, which would imply $4 trillion in balances) and was caught before the gate is the kind of catch that saves a pitch.

The self-criticism is aimed at the evidence. It is scrupulous about the numbers: the denominators, the seeds, the p-values, the corpus composition, the post-hoc vs pre-registered distinction, the CFPB split. It publishes the losses (financial distress 27/72, the 1/8, the 8th-of-9, the p=0.076, the dumb ledger). It withdraws the claims that do not survive the arithmetic (the 7-10x multiple, the $6,610 figure, the "acquiring costs 5-25x more" line). It names the things it cannot say (the $80 CAC, the UK figures, the "invisible third," the "183 lines of Python").

**Where the self-criticism stops: it is aimed at the numbers, not at the architecture.** The team is honest that the ranking does not work. It is honest that the precision is unmeasured. It is honest that the corpus is not card-specific. It is honest that the confidence float is a menu. It is honest that the CFPB churn intent is 1/8. But it is not honest — or rather, it has not yet reached the point of honesty — about what the evidence implies for the *product*. The evidence says the ranking is not the product. The evidence says the extraction and the accumulation are the product. The evidence says the brief is the output, not the score. The documents do not say this. The score is still the product. The brief is still a consumption path. The flag is still a sentence. The architecture has not been corrected, only the numbers have.

The "honesty beat" is a rhetorical device. Saying "almost every number was measured on a generic corpus" and "here's the one card number, and it's 1/8" is honest. It is also, structurally, a concession that the evidence does not support the product. The team knows this. They have written: "The single weakness is that the value claim can't be proven without their data, and no amount of synthetic work fixes that." They know. And they have responded by making the pitch about the *experiment* (the six-week back-test) rather than the *product* (the score, the queue, the model feature). The experiment is the right response to the evidence gap. But it means the pitch is "let us run a test on your data" rather than "here is the product, here is the screen, here is the flag, here is what changes on day one." The experiment is the sale. The product is the thing that comes after the experiment. The CEO is being asked to fund the experiment, not to buy the product. That is the right ask, given the evidence. But it means the product has not been sold. It has been proposed.

The self-criticism is also aimed at the things that are easiest to be honest about. The corpus limitation is easy: "we measured on the wrong corpus." The precision gap is easy: "we don't have the number." The confidence float is easy: "it's a menu." The ranking weakness is easy: "8th of 9, we publish it." The *product* gap is hard: "the thing we built is not the thing the evidence supports, and the thing the evidence supports is a different product with a different buyer and a different demo." That is not in the documents. That is the correction that would change the pitch from "let us run a back-test on your data" to "here is the screen your agents will see, here is the flag your marketing system will check, and the back-test measures whether it works." The first is a research proposal. The second is a product.

---

## 6. The choices they made

| Choice | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Attrition over pre-delinquency** | **Correct.** | The 4.5x precision-sensitivity argument is decisive. The hardship-opt-in problem is real. The $6,610 error was caught. The withdrawal is well-reasoned. The CFPB evidence (churn 1/8, complaint escalation 23/24) does not support attrition as the *strongest* direction, but attrition is the direction with the most complete evidence chain, the clearest buyer, and the most defensible demo. Pre-delinquency has better anchors but a worse T3 and a worse precision profile. Correct call. |
| **US over UK** | **Correct.** | The £650 Ombudsman tariff is a better number, but the UK market is smaller, the FCA persistent-debt argument does not translate, and the CFPB enforcement contraction makes the US regulatory argument weak. The US switch costs the best number but gains the bigger market and the more familiar currency. The £650 is kept as the answer to "is any of your value a hard number?" Correct. |
| **Head of Retention Analytics as buyer** | **Wrong for the first sale.** | As discussed in §1 and §2. The first deployment is operational. The Operations person signs. The Analytics person signs for the feature export, which is the second deployment. The CCO signs for the suppression flag, which is in the first deployment. Three buyers, two deployments. One buyer is the wrong number. |
| **Latency as headline** | **Defensible, not optimal.** | The latency claim is structurally true and unattackable in 18 minutes. The memory framing is more accurate and more durable. Use the latency sentence in minute one. Use the memory framing in the product description, the demo, and the expansion path. The latency claim is a pilot feature, not a product property. |
| **Six-week back-test as the ask** | **Correct, with one correction.** | The pre-registered criterion and walk-away are the right structure. The success criterion should be operational (disposition code change, handle time on the pilot desk) *in addition to* model-based (top-decile uplift). The operational metric justifies the first deployment. The model metric justifies the second. They have the model metric. They need the operational metric. |
| **Demo: day 0 / 74 / 132, retro column** | **Good structure, wrong climax.** | The three-conversation structure is clear. The retro column is the hardest thing to fake and it is in the demo. The "nothing here would open a case in any system you run today" line is strong. But the climax should be the agent's screen, not the score crossing. The score crossing is a system event. The agent reading the brief is a human event. Two finance executives are more moved by the human event. The demo should end on the screen: four items, one flag, one trajectory, the quote, the date. "This is what your agent sees before she picks up the phone." |
| **"The deliberately-not-selling-to-a-distressed-customer" line** | **Correct to include. Wrong to use only rhetorically.** | It is the strongest moment in the pitch. They are right to call it the single best line. But it should be a product feature (the suppression flag in the marketing platform's suppression list), not a governance sentence in Beat 4. The sentence makes the CCO feel safe. The flag makes the CCO's job easier. The flag is the product. The sentence is the description of the product. Build the flag. |
| **"The score is arithmetic, not model output"** | **True but incomplete.** | The arithmetic is deterministic. The reading is a model. The confidence float is an uncalibrated model output that is, under the production reader, the least load-bearing mechanism. The "arithmetic, not model output" claim is true for the ledger and false for the extraction. The correct claim is: "the arithmetic is deterministic and unit-tested; the reading is a model, and we promise a fingerprint, not determinism; and the confidence float is being bucketed because it is the least load-bearing thing in the score and the governance objection is valid." They get close in `06-DEFENDING-THE-SCORE.md` but the Beat 2 sentence is still the clean version, and the clean version is a half-truth. |
| **Cut list and never-cut list** | **Mostly correct.** | The "invisible third" is correctly cut (it argues against the product). The "183 lines" is correctly cut (it undersells). The five adjacent use cases are correctly cut from the stage (breadth reads as unfocus). The UK figures are correctly cut. The "7/132 - 10/132" bare pair is correctly cut. The never-cut list is right: the day-74 crossing, the retro column, the "what happens next" answer, the consumption answer, the two refusals, the honesty beat, the six-week experiment. One addition to the never-cut list: the suppression flag, once it is built. It is the CCO's product and the UDAAP answer. |
| **Reader beat as "gen-AI headline"** | **Wrong for the audience.** | The model-vs-lexicon table is the answer to "how does the reading work?" It is not the answer to "why should I buy this?" The CEO does not need the 60/65 vs 1/65 comparison. The CEO needs the agent's screen and the flag. The reader beat belongs in Q&A. The AI judge scores it separately. Putting it in the story document risks it being rehearsed and delivered as a beat, which displaces the product. |
| **Confidence float: concede, don't defend, bucket it** | **Correct.** | The "21 distinct values, 28% at 0.85" measurement is the right evidence. The "least load-bearing under the model reader" measurement is the right context. The "bucket to three tiers" recommendation is the right fix. Conceding immediately is the right tactical move. This is the best-handled weakness in the documents. |
| **SR 26-2 correction** | **Correct and critical.** | Citing SR 11-7 to a bank audience in 2026 would be the fastest way to be marked as not having checked. The correction to SR 26-2, the joint interagency framing, the $30B threshold, the GenAI scope carve-out (and the correct reading of the carve-out as "your own AI governance policy governs" rather than "there is nothing to do"): all correct. The three-tier framing (extractor / ledger / their model) is clear and defensible, with the right caveat that it is their proposed structure, not the regime's vocabulary. |
| **Model-swap as "we already did it"** | **Correct.** | "We've already changed the model and measured it, on the same 282 conversations, for under three cents" is the strongest answer to the reproducibility question. It converts an unanswerable hypothetical into a demonstrated capability. The written protocol (freeze benchmark, measure agreement, measure rank stability, re-fit calibration, report delta, champion/challenger) is the right structure. The caveat that steps 5-6 cost *their* team time is the right honesty. |

---

## The uncomfortable summary

The team built a score. The evidence says the score's ranking does not work. The team knows this. They have published the 8th-of-9, the dumb-ledger result, the p=0.076, the corpus reversals. And they have responded by making the pitch about the *experiment* rather than the *product*: "let us run a six-week back-test on your data." That is the right response to the evidence gap. It is also the response that means the product has not been sold. It has been proposed. The CEO is being asked to fund a test, not to buy a thing.

The thing that the evidence supports is the brief and the flag. The extraction works. The accumulation works. The retro re-scoring works. The quote fidelity works. The agent screen is a CRM widget. The suppression flag is a row in a table. The cost is 2 weeks of engineering plus 4-6 weeks of integration. The demo is the agent's screen, not the score crossing. The buyer is the Operations person and the CCO, not the Analytics person. The value is handle time and the email that doesn't go out, not the $1.65M/year gross ceiling.

The team has not made this shift. They are one step short. The documents say "the score is the product, the brief is a consumption path, the flag is a sentence, the buyer is Retention Analytics, the demo ends on the score crossing, the value is a chain with four haircuts." The evidence says "the score's ranking does not work, the extraction and accumulation do work, the brief is the output, the flag is the control, the buyer is Operations and Compliance, the demo ends on the screen, the value is the call that is seven minutes instead of fourteen and the email that doesn't go out."

The shift is small. It is not a rebuild. It is a re-pointing. The engine is the same. The extraction is the same. The ledger is the same. The retro re-scoring is the same. The quote-citation discipline is the same. The 908 tests are the same. What changes is: the output (brief and flag, not score and queue), the buyer (Operations and CCO, not Analytics), the demo climax (the screen, not the score crossing), the value claim (operational, not a chain), and the back-test criterion (disposition code change and handle time, in addition to top-decile uplift). The cost of the shift is a week of re-authoring the demo narrative, a day of building the suppression flag, and a re-pointing of the value chain from a margin calculation to an operational calculation. The evidence is already in the repo. The mechanism is already built. The shift is in the framing, and the framing is in the documents, and the documents are in their hands, and they have two days before the gate.

They will not make the shift in two days. They will make the pitch they have prepared. The pitch they have prepared is good. It is honest. It is well-structured. It has the right demo, the right caveats, the right ask, the right refusal to overclaim. It will land. The question is whether it lands well enough to win the shortlist, and whether the product that comes after the gate is the score and the queue or the brief and the flag. The gate decides the shortlist. The evidence should decide the product. They are not the same decision, and the team is preparing for the first one while the second one is already made by the numbers they published.
